query: Prior studies of Al-containing Cr–Co–Fe–Ni alloys showed that composition and thermal history can substantially alter constituent phases and transformation behavior, but they did not establish a predictive explanation of phase stability across the relevant thermal regime or adequately connect it to composition-dependent thermodynamic instability. Given the competing thermodynamic and kinetic factors in multicomponent alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs phase stability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially in a high-temperature BCC state and why? State a controlled comparison and baseline, predicted observations, boundary conditions, prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The phase stability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is governed by the difference in Gibbs free energies between bcc and fcc phases (ΔGbcc-fcc), which can be influenced by the composition and thermal history of the alloy.
generation.intervention: Variation of composition (e.g., changing the content of Al, Co, or Ni) or thermal history (e.g., annealing or quenching)
generation.conditions: Temperature range: 0 °C to 900 °C; Atmosphere: air or ultra-high vacuum (UHV); Strain rate: high strain rate shear
generation.structural_mediator: Stacking fault energy (SFE) of fcc phase; Laves phases; TCP structures
generation.mechanism: Thermodynamic and kinetic factors, including phase transformation kinetics, sluggish diffusion effect, and transformation volume change
generation.predicted_outcome: The alloy will exhibit a phase transformation from BCC to FCC or vice versa, depending on the composition and thermal history, resulting in changes to its mechanical properties, such as strength, hardness, and wear resistance.
generation.baseline: The initial high-temperature BCC state of the alloy
generation.boundary: The temperature range, atmosphere, and strain rate conditions
generation.uncertainty: The exact relationship between the composition, thermal history, and phase stability is still unclear and requires further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Controlled comparison of the phase stability of Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 with varying compositions (e.g., changing the content of Al, Co, or Ni) or thermal histories (e.g., annealing or quenching) using techniques such as X-ray diffraction, transmission electron microscopy, or nanoindentation
measurements: Mechanical properties (e.g., hardness, strength, wear resistance)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the phase stability of the alloy is not influenced by the composition or thermal history, as predicted by the hypothesis, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Thermodynamic ways of annealing are the common way to alter the phases in alloys. Besides the thermodynamic method, kinetics of phase transformation also greatly affects the phase selection, usually by two stages: solidification and solid-state phase transformation. The phase formation in alloys can be well controlled through the phase transformation kinetics,. For example, rapid solidification has been widely used to obtain metallic glass and solid-state phase transformation via thermal treatment has also been often employed to introduce strengthening phases in commercial alloys,,,. In spite of that the kinetics of phase transformation is well known, in HEAs, it deserves more attentions. Firstly, the phases in HEAs could be very complex because of their concentrated multi-components while phase compositions in traditional alloys are much simpler. There are two solid phases in binary alloys while five different phases at equilibrium state in the CoCrFeNiTix HEAs. It is complicated but interesting and useful to tailor the phase compositions and their volume fraction in HEAs. Secondly, it is reported that there is sluggish diffusion effect in HEAs. cited_evidence.text: To generate the fcc to bcc martensitic transformation, we adopt the following strategies: (1) to obtain a single fcc phase in the as-annealed state and (2) to increase the thermal stability of bcc phase at low temperature. It is well known that a key parameter for designing metastable MEAs as well as conventional structural alloys which show the TRIP behavior, i.e., the fcc to bcc transformation, is the stacking fault energy (SFE) of fcc. Though the SFE contains a term expressed by a difference in Gibbs free energies between hcp and fcc phases,,, the fcc to bcc transformation is also analyzed by the SFE. In this study, however, we reveal that a difference in Gibbs free energies between bcc and fcc phases can be a critical parameter for the fcc to bcc martensitic transformation. The phase equilibrium and stability were calculated by using a Thermo-Calc software along with the thermodynamic database TCFE2000 and its upgraded version. This CALPHAD approach is much more effective than trial-and-error-based conventional alloy-design approaches consuming a lot of costs and time,.
